items: Create a seasonal maintenance calendar listing tasks for each quarter and schedule your first roof inspection before spring rains arrive so you catch winter damage while it is still fixable.
Book your furnace inspection in September before the October scheduling rush because a $150 inspection can prevent a $3,000 emergency replacement during the coldest months of January.
Test smoke and carbon monoxide detectors every spring and fall while replacing batteries so these life-saving devices never fail when you and your family are sleeping.
Identify and document your main water shutoff valve location now so you can respond within seconds if a frozen pipe bursts and prevent catastrophic water damage.
Before calling anyone for a repair, first determine whether the situation is dangerous by checking for gas leaks, smoke, fire, or structural hazards that require immediate evacuation.
If your repair issue is not immediately dangerous, assess whether it is actively worsening and call a licensed plumber or structural expert for same-day service if water is involved.
Get written estimates for any contractor work exceeding $200 and refuse verbal quotes entirely, as documented agreements protect you from surprise charges and scope changes.
Before hiring any contractor, verify their license and insurance independently through your state licensing board and request three recent local references to call directly.
Set aside one to three percent of your home purchase price as an emergency reserve to cover realistic year-one costs that include HVAC servicing, roof patching, and plumbing callouts.
Budget for five common first-year expenses including HVAC servicing at $150 to $400, roof patching at $300 to $1,200, and plumbing callouts at $150 to $600 per visit.
Obtain a minimum of three written bids from licensed contractors for any repair exceeding $2,000 to ensure you are comparing competitive pricing and not overpaying.
Insist on a deposit of no more than 25 to 33 percent upfront and require the remaining payment upon completion to protect yourself from unfinished or abandoned work.
